item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles studio Ome Dezin has partnered with design platform Lumens to renovate and furnish a 1990s home in the Hollywood Hills, adding iconic furniture and lighting from Frank Gehry, Ingo Maurer and more.

Situated in middle of a mature forest on over an acre of land, the house was originally designed by architect Jeff Mills in a style that blends mid-century modern and brutalism.

The residence was once home to an A-list actor, then later converted into an art gallery, leaving white-washed walls, tall ceilings, exposed beams and expansive spaces for Ome Dezin founders Jesse Rudolph and Joelle Kutner to build upon.

"It was stripped of all personality," the duo told Dezeen. "There were no doors, bedrooms, full bathrooms, etc. It was hard for some to envision this house as a home."

They restored the original architecture, making minor alterations like adding a gym, converting an upstairs guest bedroom into the primary bathroom and erecting an exterior sauna and full bathroom.

Limestone flooring in some of the rooms was saved, while all the other surfaces were altered or added to in order to transform the property into a livable home.

"The space felt sterile when we got into it, and our goal was to bring depth, layers, and warmth to the home," the pair said.

With the surrounding forested landscape in mind, Rudolph and Kutner used wood to clad entire walls in the main living spaces and bathrooms.

They also introduced atypically tall wood baseboards to create a sense of continuity throughout the home, while stone such as richly veined marble in the bathrooms was also employed to embellish the natural aesthetic.

The kitchen is enveloped in a distinctive blue stone, while the island is clad in a rust-toned variation with an aged, tactile finish.

"Throughout the home, these earthy materials are punctuated by glimmers of jewel tones, silver, and gold — appearing in the lighting, decorative details, and custom stained-glass windows and doors we designed specifically for the space," said the team.

Read:

Willett and Ome Dezin renovate mid-century CM G1 House in LA

When it came to furnishing the residence, Ome Dezin teamed up with Lumens – a platform they already used frequently to source furniture and lighting – to choose distinctive pieces to complete the spaces.

They began with lighting, selecting favourites such as gold Ingo Maurer pendants for the kitchen, along with pieces from Foscarini and In Common With.

"Lighting is so important to us as we think of it as functional art," said Rudolph and Kutner. "It adds warmth, character, depth and shadows into a space for layer and movement."

Furniture was then layered in, from Gubi dining chairs to statement pieces like a striped Up chair by Gaetano Pesce and Frank Gehry's Wiggle Chair.

"What I love about the result is that you feel the individuality of each piece, but nothing feels overly coordinated," Lumens chief marketing officer Dana Gers told Dezeen. "There's a sense of discovery to it. It feels collected, personal and entirely at home within the architecture."

As an interior design and development studio, Ome Dezin reimagined, renovated and sold multiple properties across the greater Los Angeles area.

These include a 1960s A Quincy Jones house in Brentwood and a mid-century Laurel Hills residence for which they collaborated with furniture designer Willet.

The photography is by William Jess Laird.

item.content:encoded:
Local studio Helen & Hard has completed a timber cabin on Norway's Atlantic coast where sprawling tree-like columns made from uprooted spruce trees frame panoramic views of the sea.

Named Cabin Sande, the 112-square-metre retreat on a protected rocky headland in Randaberg occupies the footprint of a 1970s cabin. Planning restrictions required the replacement building to match the original's size and height.

Helen & Hard placed the low, angular building on a stone plinth made from rock found on site and topped it with a planted roof that follows the contours of the surrounding terrain.

The cabin is organised around 18 branching columns made from whole spruce trees, including their root systems.

Each tree was excavated with its roots intact before being cleaned, air-dried for eight months and digitally scanned, allowing robots to mill bespoke joints while preserving the organic shape of each tree.

The spruce columns spread into the ceiling like tree canopies before branching into bookshelves, benches, stairs, room dividers, window frames, doors, the kitchen and the fireplace.

Read:

Helen & Hard hangs Woodnest treehouses from pine trees above Norwegian fjord

"We wanted to evoke the experience of standing beneath a canopy of trees," Helen & Hard told Dezeen.

"As you move through the space, the rhythmic sequence of the timber columns and the organic character of the structure create a strong sense of shelter and protection."

The structural system draws on traditional Norwegian boatbuilding dating back to the Viking Age, where naturally curved joints between tree trunks and roots were used to stiffen the ribs of wooden vessels.

The fan-shaped cabin opens towards the Atlantic Ocean, where a 9.5-metre-wide window stretches across the main living space without any mullions interrupting the view.

Continuous glazing wraps around much of the cabin, bringing changing light, reflections and weather into the interior, while stepped window sills create a greater sense of enclosure away from the sea.

At the opposite end, a narrow entrance faces a sheltered garden, creating a direct sightline through the building from the vegetation behind to the sea beyond.

Two rows of cantilevered timber beams meet above the panoramic window, allowing the roof to project beyond the glazing to shelter it from the weather.

"The weather along the Atlantic coast can be extremely harsh," said the studio.

"The deep roof overhang and the arrangement of the timber structure create a sheltered, intimate place that simultaneously opens toward the sea."

A concealed system of tension cables and springs helps counteract the weight of the overhanging roof, keeping the glazed opening free from supporting columns.

The main living space sits between a kitchen and covered terrace on one side and two workspaces on the other, one raised on a half level above the bathroom.

Side spaces branch off the central room, creating more intimate places to work, cook and relax beneath the timber structure.

Founded in Stavanger in 1996 by Siv Helene Stangeland and Reinhard Kropf, Helen & Hard works across housing, cultural buildings and public projects, with a focus on timber construction and digital fabrication.

Previous projects by the studio include the Woodnest treehouses overlooking Hardangerfjord and the Vindmøllebakken co-housing development in Stavanger.

The photography is by Ivar Kvaal and Sindre Ellingsen.

item.content:encoded:
The electric vehicle market remains dominated by chunky SUVs, but some carmakers are also producing battery-powered hatchbacks that are modest in size but bold in design. Here, we round up six of the most eye-catching.

Car manufacturers continue to favour larger models for electric vehicles (EVs). They argue that the heavy batteries are more suitable for heftier cars, though some experts have also pointed out that profit margins tend to be bigger on SUVs and SUV crossovers.

But particularly in European cities, demand for more compact EVs is on the rise, with some municipalities seeking to restrict so-called "carspreading" via regulation.

As a result, we're seeing a growing group of EV hatchbacks enter the scene. Some brands have chosen simply to make electrified versions of popular combustion-engine cars – such as the Mini Cooper and the Fiat 500 – but others have taken the opportunity to experiment with a new design language.

Below, we've rounded up six production EVs that can still stand out on the street despite relatively diminutive proportions:

Hyundai Ioniq 3

Launched in April and due to go on sale in the UK and Europe later in 2026, the Ioniq 3 is described by Hyundai as an "aero hatch".

The brand says its swooping shape is determined by the natural bending behaviour of sheet steel.

It riffs directly off the Concept Three, unveiled in September 2025. Speaking to Dezeen at a media preview for the concept car, Hyundai Design Center head Simon Loasby said "we're due a renaissance" in small, cool cars.

Hyundai Inster

Also from Hyundai, though not part of its Ioniq electric sub-brand, is the Hyundai Inster. Launched in 2024, the Inster is in fact an updated, electrified version of the combustion-engine Casper, which is only available in South Korea.

The four-seater is Hyundai's smallest EV. Described by Top Gear magazine as "a cheery looker without toppling into cartoonish cuteness", it makes extensive use of the Korean carmaker's favoured pixelated lighting.

Inside, the cabin is unusually colourful, with the option of patterned upholstery.

Renault 5

Hitting showrooms in early 2025, the electric Renault 5 is a modern, battery-powered interpretation of the French carmaker's classic supermini.

It retains the distinctively angled rear hatchback of the original, which Renault produced from 1972 to 1996.

Other references to various versions of its ancestor can be found in the rear lights, the wheel arches, the bonnet vent and the dashboard.

Contemporary design twists include the A-shaped headlights and their four-cornered motif, which is repeated on the foglights and the dashboard vents.

Honda E (discontinued)

The Honda E arguably kicked off the current wave of design-forward small EVs, having been released in March 2020.

Reminiscent of the work of former Apple chief design officer Jony Ive, its emergence generated significant buzz in the car world.

But despite winning a clutch of awards it sold poorly, with reviewers bemoaning a high price point and limited range, and was ultimately discontinued by Honda in January 2024.

Honda Super N

The Honda E's effective replacement, and a reset of the Japanese manufacturer's entire approach to EVs, is the Super N.

Recently going on sale in the UK, it's a slightly sportier version of the N-One E, which launched in Japan in September 2025.

The Super N is pitched as a super-affordable option, and is in the distinctive boxy, compact style of Japan's kei cars.

Notable touches include colourful seats and simulated engine sounds and gears.

Rivian R3

The R3 is a much-hyped upcoming model from California-based EV company Rivian.

It's the only car on this list planned for availability in the US, though with no confirmation yet on when it will appear in showrooms.

Production is contingent on completion of the brand's new factory in Atlanta, Georgia, which is expected to open in 2028.

While definitely small for an American EV, the R3 will be bigger than it looks in photos. Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe has described it as "a crossover meets an SUV, meets a hatch, meets a wagon, meets a bunch of things".

The R3 will retain Rivian's distinctive face, while the brand's chief design officer, Jeff Hammoud, has claimed that its hatchback shape was inspired by 1980s rally cars such as the Audi Quattro and Lancia Delta Integrale.

item.content:encoded:
This week on Dezeen, Elon Musk announced plans to open a semiconductor factory near Houston, Texas, with a floor area of 100 million square feet that will make it the largest building in the world.

The Terafab factory, a joint chip-building venture for Musk's companies Tesla and SpaceX, will cover an area equivalent to more than 1,700 American football fields in Grimes County, if completed.

It would steal the crown from the current largest building by floor area, Russia's 65 million-square-foot (six million-square-metre) AvtoVAZ main assembly building.

In other technology news, Dezeen revealed that companies publishing realistic AI-generated architectural renderings in the European Union without labelling them risk being fined under a new law that came into force earlier this month.

"If it's realistic scenery with people walking around and it is AI generated, it will need to be labelled as AI generated," said Szymon Sieniewicz, a counsel at law firm Addleshaw Goddard.

In the US, California start-up Satyress unveiled a centaur-like robot called Threehalves, complete with a goat-shaped head.

The four-legged machine, called Threehalves, can be equipped with tools including a chainsaw and remote operated to take on demanding jobs that would put humans at risk of harm.

Automotive company Jaguar has shared a first look at the interior of its upcoming Type 01 electric car – the production version of the controversial Type 00 concept unveiled in 2024.

Renders of the interior show a central divider that runs the full length of the car, effectively separating all of the seats.

In architecture news, UK practice Heatherwick Studio has unveiled scaled-back plans for its redevelopment of an elevated waterfront park in Louisville, Kentucky.

The updated design for the Belvedere park extends green spaces across an existing overpass over a six-lane highway, but is much less ambitious than the original undulating design unveiled by the studio last year due to expense and safety concerns.

Projects that turned our readers' heads this week included a crystal-shaped sauna in Sweden, a cedar-wrapped gallery on a secluded Washington island and a mass-timber groundscraper in Auckland that resembles a "continuous ribbon".

item.content:encoded:
Social media platform Instagram has updated its brand identity with elements such as a refreshed, "bolder and simpler" wordmark and updated typographic elements across the platform.

The update was announced this week and is rolling out globally through 2026 and beyond. Designed in-house, the refresh introduces "something to carry us into the future," said technology company Meta, which owns the platform.

The most notable change is the Instagram wordmark, which has remained the same since 2016. It maintains its cursive, with the serifs have been flattened and detached from the neighbouring letter.

The team said the wordmark pays homage to crafted script to reflect the creativity of Instagram.

"Script reflects individuality, so referencing that felt right," said Instagram director of product design Jasmine Probst.

"The new wordmark is bolder and simpler, with touches of unexpectedness. It cues individual expression, a personal voice, both of which have always been core to Instagram".

Other updates include new typography rolled out across the app, with the platform's gradient colours integrated in "subtle" ways. Motion, layout and UI will also be updated as part of the brand refresh.

Read:

The top rebrands of 2025

In a post from the Instagram Design account, the team said it explored "hundreds of directions" before arriving at something "fresh and simple".

Instagram head Adam Mosseri said it was "time for a refresh" in another recent post on the platform.

"The refreshed brand system puts our community's creativity and self-expression front and center," said Meta director of brand design May Hartono.

"It's designed to spark courageous action and give people the confidence to create and show up as themselves, freely and fully."

Other major technology companies have rebranded in recent years, including Amazon and Google.

It follows a more subtle approach to rebranding seen across these mega corporations, where design changes are almost imperceptible. Dezeen recently rounded up five such projects.

Other companies have taken a bolder approach, such as the American eatery Cracker Barrel, which was met with an explosion of internet backlash.

The images are courtesy of Meta

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Populous has completed the steep, metal-clad Highmark Stadium in Buffalo, New York for NFL team the Buffalo Bills, with a canopy and advanced snow-melt system.

The new Highmark Stadium replaces a structure of the same name that is located just across the street in Orchard Park, Buffalo. It opened for the season this past weekend for a training event attended by the team and fans.

The design of the stadium, which features an open-air bowl covered slightly by a steel canopy, is intended to enhance noise within the interior and also protect fans from the city's 95 inches of annual snowfall and other inclement weather.

The majority of the exterior is wrapped in grey semi-translucent perforated metal panels, which wrap an inner 360-degree colonnade populated with concessions.

A dark grey brick features at the structure's base, and the Highmark wordmark features on each aspect.

Inside, the stadium seating is steeper than its predecessor and was designed to bring fans closer to the field.

The canopy itself dips downwards along the stadium's side and rises towards the middle. The roof is outfitted with an extensive hydronic snow-melt system, which will help melt and irrigate snowfall to protect the events below.

Read:

Eight record-breaking stadiums from the biggest to the most expensive

Overall, according to the studio, the design was informed by the historic architecture of Buffalo, such as the Rockpile, the city's former outdoor soccer stadium.

Its towering stainless steel buffalo sculptures were created by artist Blessing Hancock.

The stadium took three years to construct.

Upon its recent opening, some fans took issue with obstructed views at their seats, according to reports.

Populous global director and managing director Jonathan Mallie told local outlet the Buffalo News the obstructed views are a result of creating a higher stacked stadium that would bring fans closer to the field.

"You will find some level of obstruction in every stadium in the world," said Mallie.

"The goal was to bring everybody closer to the field and create an upper deck with an incredible proximity and presence within the bowl to help create a next-level experience for Bills Mafia."

Further images are forthcoming.

Dezeen recently explored the future of stadium design in its Future Stadium series, including why stadium architecture is getting more outlandish and what they may look like in decades to come, according to nine architects.

The images are by Tim McManus, courtesy of Populous.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a proposal to reimagine a former industrial mill in the Lake District as a place where ecology, heritage and community converge is among the student projects from the University of Northumbria.

Also featured is a maritime repair and recycling hub, and a proposal to transform a Grade II listed building into a space to promote textile reuse.

Institution: Northumbria University
School: School of Architecture and Built Environment
Course: BA (Hons) Architecture, PG Cert Interior Architecture, BA Hons Interior Architecture, DA Architecture
Tutor: Cameron McEwan

School Statement:

"At Northumbria University, we test ideas about how architecture can respond to a turbulent world, engaging the multidimensional pressures of our moment, from the climate crisis and resource scarcity to rapid urban change.

"Our school is home to academics who have generated extensive knowledge into design studio practices locally and globally, embedding situated, hands-on learning throughout the curriculum.

"We cultivate architect-citizens who can move fluidly across drawing, writing, making, and authentic learning from live projects. Newcastle and its region form our primary critical tool, grounding projects in the region’s distinctive character and heritage.

"We study the totality of the city, reading its continuities and disruptions, histories and typologies.

"We work from room to territory, and students develop projects by thinking-through-making, using typology as both analytical and projective, as a way of situating design in the material reality of our shared context while speculating on what might yet be imagined and built.

"To follow the School of Architecture and Built Environment on Instagram, follow @nu_architecture and @nu_interiorarch."

Auter by Chris Hemsley

"Auter is a proposal for a new cultural instrument embedded within central Newcastle's urban fabric, honouring the site as a palimpsest continually rewritten through inhabitation, memory and transformation.

"Conceived as a temporal artefact within a temporal landscape, the design operates as an urban infrastructure and performance space, dissolving boundaries between audience and spectacle – production and consumption.

"Resisting the comfort that defines many contemporary cultural venues, Auter uses discomfort and spatial friction to provoke participation.

"Several stereotomic concrete forms, expressing permanence and memory, interplay with a tectonic scaffold grate framework of adaptability and reinterpretation. Auter proposes a living, continuously re-authored memory theatre."

Student: Chris Hemsley
Course: BA Hons Architecture
Tutor: Tara Hipwood
Email: hemsleyhemsleyhemsley[at]gmail.com

Beyond the Bottle by Eve Capstick

"A civic landscape for maritime repair, reuse, and the continuation of the Tyne's working heritage. Ship launches, traditionally marked by the breaking of a glass bottle against the hull, are well documented throughout the maritime archives of South Shields.

"However, far less attention is given to the later life of these vessels beyond their departure from the river.

"Each year, hundreds of boats reach the end of their operational life, many dismantled under unsafe conditions or abandoned entirely.

"In response, this project proposes a contemporary maritime repair and recycling hub that reconsiders the afterlife of boats through repair, reuse, education and public engagement.

"Transforming a former dry dock into an infrastructure for environmental renewal."

Student: Eve Capstick
Course: BA Hons Architecture
Tutor: Kyung Wook Seo

Unpicking: MEA House by Bernadette Renshaw

"This proposal reimagines MEA House's historic role as a charitable hub by transforming it into a sanctuary for wellbeing and textile reuse.

"The spatial strategy involves stripping the Grade II listed building back to its base structure, revealing these historical layers and creating open, shared volumes, which foster a deeply convivial atmosphere.

"This 'reset' spatially mirrors the tactile act of textile repair and incorporates elements of textile reuse.

"The scheme prioritises the sensory and lived qualities of interior space, offering a place for the local community where connection is prioritised."

Student: Bernadette Renshaw
Course: BA Hons Interior Architecture
Tutors: Andrea Couture, Paul Ring and Rachel Currie

Reset: The Next Page by Connie Darnell

"This project explores a process-led approach to civic interior architecture through the transformation of paper waste within MEA House.

"The proposal is informed by the building's stripped-back material condition, where exposed stud walls and torn plasterboard revealed interiors that felt paper-thin within a concrete and steel structure.

"Developed through material experimentation, it tests the reuse potential of everyday paper waste and translates these findings into spatial, material and community-led interventions.

"A visible loop system enables waste paper to be collected, pulped, remade and reused as journals and other resources. Transforming disposal into collective production.

"By combining material research, participatory making and principles of material reuse, the project reimagines waste as a shared civic asset while demonstrating how experimentation can directly inform spatial outcomes and community engagement."

Student: Connie Darnell
Course: BA Hons Interior Architecture
Tutors: Andrea Couture, Paul Ring and Rachel Currie

Alphabetti Theatre by Amber Morley

"The project reimagines the theatre as a civic destination where performance extends beyond the stage and into everyday public life.

"Guided by the metaphor of "behind the scenes," the design reveals the hidden processes of making, rehearsing and performing, transforming spaces traditionally concealed from the public into opportunities for engagement and learning.

"Inspired by stagecraft, rhythm and pause, the spatial sequence encourages exploration and interaction.

"Located within Newcastle Upon Tyne, the proposal responds sensitively to its historic context through adaptive reuse and sustainable design, creating an inclusive cultural hub where performers, makers and visitors become part of the theatrical experience."

Student: Amber Morley
Course: PG Cert Interior Architecture
Tutors: Peter Dixon and Laura Brown

Reimagining Alphabetti Theatre by Daniel Bell

"The project inserts a new performance volume within the existing structure, extending theatre into a tiered public landscape.

"The stepped terrain operates as an external auditorium, encouraging gathering and informal performance throughout the day.

"By blurring the boundary between inside and outside, the proposal transforms Alphabetti into an open civic platform for performance, interaction and community engagement."

Student: Daniel Bell
Course: PG Cert Interior Architecture
Tutors: Peter Dixon and Laura Brown

A Pier with Purpose by Peter Blevins

"At Skegness, a Victorian pier is extended 650 metres into the North Sea as an inhabited structural landscape.

"Two ribbons of steel, drawn from the wake of a seal moving through kelp, diverge and rejoin to generate plan, section and structure as a single continuous logic.

"Their geometry houses a maritime rescue station, a circular lido and marina, and a thalassotherapy spa, connected by a cable car.

"Rather than applying architecture to engineering, the scheme treats structure itself as spatial narrative, where load path, material honesty and programme are inseparable. The pier becomes both civic infrastructure and a choreographed journey."

Student: Peter Blevins
Course: DA Architecture
Tutor: Paul Jones
Email: peter.w.blevins[at]northumbria.ac.uk

Newcastle Stories by Ellie Owen

"Located in the heart of the city, Newcastle Stories proposes a new civic landmark: a dedicated place for people to come together, learn and share cultures and experiences.

"Political division and the decline of publicly funded institutions have eroded local communities. Newcastle Stories responds through architectural intervention, encouraging the mixing of communities and supporting those most affected.

"At its core, the project provides education to all, building social cohesion and repair.

"The scheme reimagines the 1960s landmark buildings around Princess Square through four strands: a healthy food canteen; a museum and archives; a library of radical literature; and workshops for affordable arts and design access."

Student: Ellie Owen
Course: MArch Architecture
Tutors: Will Campbell and Lesley McIntyre

The Lithic Institute of Landscape and Material Ecology by Lucy Barrett

"The Lithic Institute is a living learning environment, where knowledge is discovered through contact with the land itself.

"Along a Durham coastline shaped by erosion, industry and abandonment, it calls for a culture of environmental attention grounded in exchange rather than extraction.

"Wind, tide and stone become instruments of instruction, understood through texture, weight and time rather than abstracted data.

"With only 21 per cent of disadvantaged young people here progressing to higher education, compared with 32 per cent inland, the institute reframes learning as communal practice, uniting walkers, residents, students and scientists in shared observation, recording and making, cultivating a collective literacy of place."

Student: Lucy Barrett
Course: MArch Architecture
Tutors: Will Campbell and Lesley McIntyre

Edgeland by Lauren Cunningham

"‘Edgeland reimagines Millom's former industrial landscape as a place where ecology, heritage and community converge.

"Positioned on the periphery of the Lake District, between land and sea, industry and nature, the project proposes a new interpretation centre, habitat creation and a regenerative masterplan for RSPB Hodbarrow.

"Inspired by the sea defences that shape the site, its fractured monolithic architecture embodies a continual ballet of resistance and surrender between humanity and nature.

"As the landscape gradually reclaims the built form, the project becomes both a celebration of ecological renewal and a catalyst for Millom's future."

Student: Lauren Cunningham
Course: DA Architecture
Tutor: Paul Jones

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen Showroom: from lampshades and beds to chairs and kitchens, the following wooden products are all listed in our Showroom section.

Timber has been used in the production of furnishings for thousands of years thanks to its durability, ease of access, straightforward woodworking techniques and aesthetic appeal.

Contemporary design brands and craftspeople are still opting to use it for their designs, with popular species including ash, walnut, oak and birch plywood.

Read on to find out more about some of the recent wooden pieces we've published on Dezeen Showroom.

Adinne chair by Leonardo Rossano for True Design

Tube-shaped legs and a slab-like seat in solid ash, walnut or oak comprise this stocky chair by architect and designer Leonardo Rossano for Italian brand True Design.

The Adinne chair's timber materiality is complemented by a stiff leather strap that acts as a backrest stretched between the rear uprights.

Find out more about Adinne ›

Contemporary Room Dividing Screens by Fold Studio

A trio of interconnected wooden frames, secured with raw brass hinges, create the structure for these three-panelled screens.

Created by Australian design brand Fold Studio, users can select either rattan or fabric panels and ash, walnut or oak for the frames.

Find out more about Contemporary Room Dividing Screens ›

Modular kitchens by Vermland

Copenhagen-based interior design studio Vermland's modular kitchens are handmade in Denmark and made out of solid oak.

The cabinetry's warm-toned wooden materiality, minimal Scandi aesthetic and high-quality hardware were chosen with the intention of creating a timeless piece.

Find out more about Vermland's modular kitchens ›

Theo folding chair by Matteo Thun and Benedetto Fasciana for Plank

Italian architect Matteo Thun and designer Benedetto Fasciana worked together to create a minimalist wooden folding chair for Italian furniture brand Plank.

The Theo folding chair is made from a combination of plywood and oak veneer, which can be painted in a number of colours.

Find out more about Theo ›

Adilo pendant lamp by Ilkka Kauppinen for Secto Design

Designer Ilkka Kauppinen designed the sculptural Adilo pendant lamp with a birch plywood structure – available in two sizes – that fans out from flat.

item.content:encoded:
Local architecture studio Mosley Thorold has updated and extended a Victorian home in east London, using a textured palette of concrete, brick, tiles and metal intended to patina over time.

Named De Beauvoir Townhouse after the neighbourhood in which it is located, Mosley Thorold renovated the two-storey home and added a rear extension that reorients its layout towards a generous garden.

"So many of these houses prioritise the front elevation, the arrival, the public face, inherently – it's all about curb appeal," co-founder Nathan Mosley told Dezeen.

"We wanted to turn that logic inward, so that the garden becomes the primary event rather than an afterthought glimpsed from the back windows," he added.

Two key spatial gestures defined the project. The first was the repositioning of the home's staircase to the rear of the home, where it borrows light and views from a full-height window next to a library with raised ceilings.

The second is a large kitchen and dining area specifically requested by the client for large gatherings, which is organised around a custom dining table designed by Mosley Thorold. This room opens out onto the garden patio via a set of folding doors made from reclaimed shutters.

Steel columns and beams painted a deep reddish-brown frame the extension's interiors, designed as part of a structure to support the formwork of its poured concrete walls without putting strain on the existing party wall.

The tactility of this rough concrete has been complemented externally by weathered metal window frames, and internally by timber ceilings and a checkered floor made from reclaimed cement tiles.

Read:

Will Gamble Architects adds "explicitly tropical" extension to Grade-II listed English cottage

For the living spaces, bedrooms and bathrooms on the home's upper floors, this palette has been translated into walls painted in earthy shades, dark wood floors and concrete basins.

"We wanted materials with an inviting, tactile quality, things you want to touch, as much as look at, but equally we were thinking long term about how they'd age," Mosley said.  "Materials that develop a patina rather than simply wear out."

"Victorian buildings were crafted by hand, and there's a real celebration of what materials could do embedded in that era of building," Mosley added.

"I think contemporary design can carry the same spirit, even if the tools have changed entirely."

Mosley Thorold worked with garden designer Sophie Gordon for the home's garden, which steps up from the lower patio to a lawn lined by salvaged brick beds for planting.

Perpendicular to the main garden, a formerly underutilised strip of land has also been transformed with a natural swimming pool, overlooked by a sauna and changing area finished in rough stone and black timber.

Elsewhere in De Beauvoir, interiors firm Irenie Studio recently collaborated with architect Studio Dera to update a 19th-century townhouse, while Architecture For London added a light-filled extension to a Victorian home.

The photography is by Ollie Tomlinson.

item.content:encoded:
Spanish studio Typsa Arquitectura has completed a library in Luanda, Angola, with a curving concrete roof punctured by openings that encircle existing trees on the site.

Located at the centre of Luanda's technology park, the 1,915-square-metre library was designed around the site's existing mature trees, which determined its footprint, spatial organisation and roof design.

Rather than clearing the plot, Typsa Arquitectura organised the library around a series of planted courtyards, allowing the existing trees to become part of the design.

"Across cultures and throughout history, the shade of a tree has provided a natural place for gathering, learning, exchange and rest," lead architect Marina González Suárez told Dezeen.

"The mature trees became the project's primary design generator," added Suárez.

"Instead of defining the building first and adapting the landscape afterwards, the architecture grew around them."

The library is capped by a curving concrete roof that swells and narrows across the site before opening into circular voids that frame the retained trees.

Supported by a structural system of reinforced concrete slabs and slender steel columns, the roof extends beyond the glazed facades to create deep shaded walkways and broad cantilevers.

Typsa Arquitectura said the trees informed the placement of the courtyards and the building's fluid plan, which replaces conventional corridors with gently curving circulation routes that loop around the planted spaces.

The roof also forms the centrepiece of the library's passive environmental strategy. Separated from the occupied spaces below, it is a ventilated double-layered roof that allows air to circulate continuously, dissipating heat before it reaches the interiors.

Read:

Snøhetta creates library to emulate feeling of "sitting under a tree"

Together with cross-ventilation and the shade provided by the trees, the roof reduces solar gain and helps to create a cooler environment.

The curved glass facades are shaded by tall, adjustable brise soleil screens that pivot according to the sun's orientation.

The brise soleil fins are made of lacquered aluminium and give the elevations a slightly irregular texture.

According to the studio, this system reinterprets the brise soleil commonly found in Angolan modernist architecture, while filtering daylight to cast shifting grid-like shadows across the library's curved white interiors.

Inside, white walls, polished floors and floor-to-ceiling glazing create bright, open interiors animated by shifting shadows cast through the perforated screens.

The library is organised across two public floors, with an additional technical level dedicated to building services.

Visitors enter at ground level, where the main entrance leads into reading areas, administrative offices and a multipurpose auditorium.

A broad central timber staircase ascends to the upper floor, where the principal reading room extends onto a terrace overlooking the surrounding park.

"The sequence of spaces has been designed to encourage an intuitive and relaxed experience," said project director Joaquin Beltran Del Corral.

"Rather than following a linear route, visitors move through a series of interconnected environments that gradually reveal different views, scales and activities."

Founded in Madrid in 1966, Typsa Arquitectura is the architecture division of engineering consultancy Typsa. The practice designs civic, educational, transport and infrastructure projects across Europe, Africa and the Middle East.

Another library designed to emulate the feeling of sitting under a tree is Beijing City Library in China, featuring towering tree-like columns.

Also recently featured on Dezeen was The MAAK's Rahmah Library in Cape Town, where bricks made from Apartheid-era demolition rubble were incorporated into the building.

item.content:encoded:
A study has found that children living in Star Homes, a housing initiative in Tanzania, have lower rates of malaria, diarrhoea and respiratory infections compared to those living in mud-and-thatch houses.

The study, which was published in Nature Medicine, found that cases of malaria in children were 44 per cent lower for children residing in Star Home residences, diarrhoea was 30 per cent less and acute respiratory infections were reduced by 18 per cent.

The research also found that children living in Star Homes had greater height-for-age growth trajectories, indicating a reversal of stunting, which is a consequence of repeated childhood infection.

Star Homes was designed by representatives of the Royal Danish Academy, which also co-authored the study, in collaboration with Tanzanian and international researchers.

The study was carried out over three years by Tanzanian research group CSK Research Solutions, Tanzania's Ifakara Health Institute, the Mahidol-Oxford Tropical Medicine Research Unit at the University of Oxford, Durham University in the UK, Amsterdam University Medical Center, University of the Philippines Manila and East, Central and Southern Africa Health Community.

Taking place between January 2022 and December 2024, it looked at children under the age of 13 living across 70 villages in rural Mtwara, Tanzania.

Through a randomised public lottery of over 14,600 surveyed homes, a group of children living in 110 Star Homes was compared to children living in 513 traditional mud-and-thatch houses.

In the study, researchers argued that the contraction of the three preventable yet deadly diseases – malaria, diarrhoea and respiratory infections – is closely linked to the home environment, where children spend a large portion of their days.

It highlighted poor ventilation, overcrowding, poor sanitation and insufficient access to clean water as contributing to the spread of pathogens and airborne infections in the home.

Designed by the Royal Danish Academy in collaboration with Tanzanian and international researchers, Star Homes houses have a two-storey prefabricated structure that uses passive engineering strategies to help with disease prevention.

Bedrooms are positioned on the upper floor to avoid mosquitoes, which are more commonly found at ground level.

Net walls let air in and help with cross-ventilation, keeping sleeping areas cool while keeping mosquitoes out, and screened windows and self-closing doors further prevent insects from entering.

The houses have solar-powered lighting and are built atop an elevated, easy-to-clean concrete floor. Rainwater harvesting provides safe drinking water, a cooking stove vents smoke to the outdoors, and the toilet is a fly-proof, ventilated latrine.

Read:

Architectural Pioneering Consultants and Wolfgang Rossbauer use local materials for a school in Tanzania

"What is groundbreaking about the project is that architecture is incorporated as an active component of a randomised clinical trial and measured with the same level of rigour as medical research," said Star Homes architect and Royal Danish Academy dean Jakob Brandtberg Knudsen.

"What is crucial to our research is not architecture alone, but the interdisciplinary collaboration between architects, social scientists, physicians, biologists, and statisticians," he continued.

"Architecture can function as a health intervention on a par with medicine when it is developed and documented using scientific methods, while at the same time saving resources and reducing carbon emissions."

According to the study, the material cost of a Star Homes house is 24 per cent less than a typical single-storey cement-block house, and it generates 57 per cent less embodied carbon.

The study's authors described it as "the first-ever randomised controlled trial using a house as an intervention", and hope it encourages the building of disease-preventative, low-carbon homes across Africa.

"Our ground-breaking study shows that building better can turn a dangerous home into a safe one by protecting children in sub-Saharan Africa against three major killer diseases," said study author Steve Lindsay, professor of biosciences at Durham University.

"Based on decades of research, this was the first clinical trial of a purpose-built healthy house, and the findings are very exciting," he continued.

"We now hope that the building industry will adopt some of the important features of our healthy house design that are protective, cheaper and use less carbon than conventional concrete African houses."

Other projects in Tanzania that have featured on Dezeen include a school made from local materials, which won architecture project of the year in Dezeen Awards 2023, and a school arranged around a tree-filled courtyard.

The photography is by Julien Lanoo and the video is by Sava Films.

item.content:encoded:
Interior design practice Busta Studio has filled the Kimpton Ashbel hotel on Park Avenue with art and objects intended to make it feel like "a warm, elegantly curated home".

Located in a 1928 beaux-arts building on New York City's famous Park Avenue, Kimpton Ashbel was designed to feel like a private residence.

"Park Avenue is one of New York City's most iconic streets, instantly evoking the elegance of its heritage townhouses," Busta Studio founder Anna Busta told Dezeen.

"Drawing from this distinctive spirit, we envisioned a conceptual townhouse experience – welcoming guests into a warm, elegantly curated home."

Anna and her husband Jonathan Busta, who run Busta Studio together, used hand-brushed blonde limed oak panelling and arches juxtaposed with Bianco Dolomiti and Pietra marbles to create the right feel for the interior.

The studio also combined hand-cast bronze, glass, inlaid bronze and hand-cut mosaic stone with white plaster ceilings and mouldings for a deliberately simple yet elegant look.

"The New York townhouse concept itself is an endless source of inspiration: a place where one lingers, surrounded by bespoke millwork, refined finishes, stylish furnishings, and a curated mix of art and collected objects that feel personal and storied," Jonathan Busta told Dezeen.

To create privacy from the bustle of Park Avenue, custom louvres were added at street level.

Guests are welcomed by a custom inlaid mosaic featuring the hotel's KA initials when entering the lobby, which Busta Studio filled with specially commissioned artworks and decorative objects.

Read:

A-nrd designs Arthouse Glasgow hotel to "feel like it belongs to the city"

"We curated the art collection to create a nice, easy vibe for the interior, with a mixture of graphics, original paintings, photography and sculpture," Anna Busta said.

"All pieces are specifically commissioned for the space, and the overall collection has a simple but sophisticated guiding aesthetic," she continued. "We didn't want to provoke with art, but instead we simply embraced beauty."

The designers wanted to tie the communal spaces and guestrooms at Kimpton Ashbel together by using a coherent colour palette for the hotel, which focuses on calming neutral hues juxtaposed with jewel colours.

"Jewel tones inject vibrancy into accent pieces like arch chairs, side stools, headboards, and art chairs, striking a harmonious balance between subtle and bold statements that add warmth and approachability to the space," Jonathan Busta said.

To create a homely feeling, Busta Studio used velvets, linens, naturally tanned leathers and boucle fabrics.

The studio said it hoped that the mix of tactile materials, refined finishes and well-considered artworks would create a feeling that is reminiscent of a well-designed home.

"We believe the guest experience is enhanced by this intimate approach," Anna Busta concluded.

Other hotels recently featured on Dezeen include a Glasgow hotel in a 19th-century townhouse and a Tokyo boutique hotel designed to feel like staying at the home of a friend.

The photography is courtesy of Kimpton Ashbel.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: atmospherically dark glass and seamless surfaces take centre stage in appliance brand Fisher & Paykel's Minimal Style kitchen products, designed to help build spaces with visual calm and formal rigour.

The Minimal appliances are one of three product design styles in Fisher & Paykel's luxury range, alongside Contemporary and Professional offerings.

The Minimal kitchen line includes handle- and dial-free ovens and flush-fitting cooktops, all designed with the same aim: to sit quietly within the kitchen and support continuous surface planes.

The Minimal appliances are set in contrast to the more expressive lines, brushed silver glass finish and defined controls of the Contemporary range. Together, both are designed to bring the "beauty of choice" to architects, designers and homeowners in the luxury market, according to Fisher & Paykel.

For the Minimal range, the New Zealand company focused not just on simplicity but the deeper formal goals of minimalism, applying scrutiny to "every line, proportion, material junction and surface transition" to reach an essential expression.

At the same time, its designers aspired to beauty, seeking to find poetry in the relationships between surfaces, finishes, light and shadow.

"As kitchens have become more central to the architecture of the home, expectations around integration and refinement have continued to evolve," said Fisher & Paykel head of industrial design (cooking) Adam Moody.

"Advances in materials, connectivity and manufacturing precision are allowing minimalist principles to be realised with new levels of precision and sophistication."

Fisher & Paykel's vision for the Minimal Style kitchen involves combining its ovens, hobs and complementary luxury cooking appliances with integration, concealing refrigeration, wine and dishwashing solutions behind cabinetry to build a calm and cohesive space.

To make the visible appliances contribute to the aesthetic, they are made of black or grey glass, giving them both an atmospheric presence and a sense that they are fading into the background. This also gives designers more freedom to explore colour, material and texture elsewhere in the space.

Seamless finishes are also prioritised, with flush installation, very fine two-millimetre perimeter gaps and designs that are free of handles or dials that would otherwise disrupt the surface plane.

"Where appliances remain visible, the visually recessive qualities of the style extend the intention of integration," said Moody. "It's an approach that draws on enduring principles of minimalist architecture and industrial design: find the essence of an object, then celebrate its form and tactility."

The designers have paid attention to detail to heighten the luxury quality of the products, including elements such as the movement of the oven door, the precise edge detailing and a picture-frame effect giving depth to the oven front.

Large, high-resolution touchscreen displays are designed for responsiveness, while voice control enables easy multitasking, and integration with the SmartHQ connected-home platform allows for remote control and monitoring.

Fisher & Paykel's Minimal Style is available in a range of steam assist, combination steam and convection ovens in 60- and 76-centimetre formats. Companion products like warming drawers, vacuum drawers for sous-vide preparation, and integrated coffee makers are also available.

Fisher & Paykel launched the Minimal Style line alongside its State of the Art collection at EuroCucina during Milan design week 2026.

The company was founded in New Zealand in 1934. Find out more about the brand and its Minimal Style luxury appliances on its website.

item.content:encoded:
German studio Sauerbruch Hutton and US practice Studio Gang have been selected to redesign German House to reflect the nation's values and create a "civic landmark" just north of the United Nations complex in Manhattan.

Selected by a jury, the redesign will see the recladding and interior redesign of the 325-foot-tall (99-metre-tall) skyscraper, which was originally designed by American studio SLCE Architects in the 1990s and serves as a base of operations for the Consulate General of the Federal Republic of Germany.

Sauerbruch Hutton and Studio Gang, design architect and architect of record, respectively, conceived a structure with bands of colour on the facade, brightening the current grey exterior.

The studios are combining civic presence and technical efficiency to "display the latest German engineering in sustainable construction before a global audience", according to the team.

"We look forward to working with the Bundesbau Baden-Württemberg and Sauerbruch Hutton to help reimagine German House as a more welcoming and sustainable model for civic architecture in New York and within the international diplomatic community," said Studio Gang founding partner Jeanne Gang.

"This project, which holds cultural exchange at its heart, is an exciting opportunity to bring together German design expertise with the proven project delivery in New York City."

The team plans to integrate photovoltaic panels onto the facade while formulating a box-window system that allows for solar shading and the opening of windows to allow for natural ventilation.

These interventions will be made while maintaining the heightened security necessary for a high-profile diplomatic building.

The team also plans to revamp the interior spaces, integrating a "sky lobby with a vertical garden" at mid-tower, which will serve as a meeting point for the Consulate General and the UN mission.

Read:

Eero Saarinen's Black Rock skyscraper refurbished in New York

A restaurant on the upper floors will open onto a shaded garden space.

The choice of renovating, as opposed to building new, was also highlighted by the studios, which noted the carbon benefits of preserving the structure.

"Through careful transformation rather than replacement, the tower is adapted to encourage exchange across departments while extending the life of the building for decades to come," said Sauerbruch Hutton partner Lina Lahiri.

The building will be the first project by Sauerbruch Hutton in the United States.

Other recent Manhattan skyscraper renovations include SOM's renovation of the iconic Lever House and Vocon Architects and MdeAS Architects' renovation of Eero Saarinen's Black Rock skyscraper.

item.content:encoded:
New York architecture studio Diller Scofidio + Renfro has spliced an 1894 brick warehouse building with several glazed volumes to create a home for MIT's School of Architecture and Planning.

The Metropolitan Storage Warehouse building (MET) is located on the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) campus in Cambridge, Massachusetts and will house several architecture and design schools, including the Department of Architecture and the Department of Urban Studies and Planning.

The schools will relocate to the converted warehouse from their current location in the neoclassical Building 7, which sits cady corner to the new building.

Originally built in 1894 by local architect Frederic Pope and expanded throughout the decades, the brick warehouse once stored items such as pianos, carriages and furs for Boston's wealthiest families.

The studio's renovation included expanding the building's low ceiling heights and inserting "a series of carved-out voids" along the building's length, while maintaining portions of the original brick facade.

The project included careful "cutting strategies" and the application of new support systems to shift existing loads within the building to make room for modern academic spaces such as studios and makerspaces.

"By creating the necessary high-ceiling studio spaces through the removal of portions of the heavy, archaic masonry floor system, the structural load imposed on the existing columns and wood piles was significantly reduced," said Diller Scofidio + Renfro (DS+R).

"This reduction revealed sufficient reserve capacity within the existing structure to support the newly introduced, lightweight modern floor slabs, which are 'hung' by steel straps from beams supported by the existing columns and wood piles."

This architectural surgery allowed for a light, open, majority column-free interior and was informed by the interventions of Gordon Matta-Clark, according to the studio.

On the interior, the studio left some of the cuttings exposed to showcase the historical cross-sections to students. This can be seen in the sections of the original brick archways that run underneath the floor slabs.

Read:

MIT researchers design Heirloom House concrete components to last "1,000 years"

The programming and studios are now organised around large, double-height spaces, which are traversed via a continuous linear public stair.

They are organised into "neighbourhoods" across the five interconnected volumes of the building. Along one facade of the building, the glass insertions are exposed, while the other side is completely brick.

The studio also maintained details such as the building's fortress-like corner towers and crenellated corbeled cornices, while punching new windows into its two-foot-thick walls.

The team is targeting LEED Gold for the project.

"The techniques used in this adaptive reuse project have a pedagogical objective  –  to expose layers of history and allow students to experience firsthand the possibilities of breathing new life into a relic previously thought to be uninhabitable," said the studio.

DS+R recently adapted a London hangar into a publicly accessible storage facility for the Victoria and Albert Museum in London and is also working on a mass timber building at Boston University.

item.content:encoded:
Indian studio AKSH Architects has completed The Earthen Retreat, a cluster of guesthouses in Pune created by repurposing several small abandoned buildings and coating them with mud and lime plaster.

The 557-square-metre plot was previously occupied by four site offices and storage units that had outlived their original purpose.

While maintaining the existing timber and steel structures of these units, AKSH Architects used natural materials to demonstrate how "forgotten infrastructure" can be transformed into "architecture with lasting cultural, environmental and experiential value".

"The design intervention was intentionally radical," the studio's founder Akash Shingvi told Dezeen.

"Every space was reshaped through sculptural forms, natural mud and lime-plastered surfaces, local materials and fluid spatial planning, making it almost impossible to recognise the original buildings," added Shingvi.

"Our intention was to create an experience that feels timeless, earthy and deeply connected to nature, where architecture is perceived through texture, light and emotion rather than ornamentation."

The four blocks, each of which is divided into two neighbouring guesthouses, are arranged symmetrically around a communal paved patio with a swimming pool at its centre.

Inside, each of The Earthen Retreat's guesthouses contains a bedroom and a bathroom that has been left partially open to the elements, sheltered by a bamboo canopy that allows light and air to filter through.

Read:

Eleena Jamil shades Malaysian guesthouse with bamboo and steel canopy

Textured, lime-plastered walls and ceilings envelop the rooms, finished in earthy shades of beige and dark green, and punctured by arched and curved openings.

Curved forms were also used for built-in benches that extend around half of the bedrooms to form bedside tables, as well as for the bathroom's large, oval-shaped bath and a curved opening into the shower.

Externally, each of the four units has been given a matching rough plaster finish, with their perimeters shaded by the deep overhang of the bamboo roofs above.

"Curved, organic forms replace rigid partitions, allowing movement through the cottage to feel fluid, intuitive and experiential," said Shingvi.

"Since the retreat sits in a tropical setting, it didn't feel right to introduce materials that looked overly refined or disconnected from the place," he added.

"We consciously worked with natural materials that were commonly available in the local context, such as bamboo, lime and mud plaster and timber," he added.

Other projects in India that have recently incorporated mud and earth into their material palette include Aurva Illam near Hyderabad, a home by studio Iki Builds designed to reflect the rocky character of the nearby Deccan Plateau, and the mud-walled Winterfell house, which is woven around existing trees in Tamil Nadu.

The photography is by Harsh Lunavat.

item.content:encoded:
British carmaker Jaguar has revealed a glimpse of its upcoming Type 01 electric car, which has a central divider and "on-demand" screens.

The recently released renders show the interior of Jaguar's Type 01 electric car, which will be the production version of the much-discussed Type 00 concept car that was first revealed in 2024.

Jaguar plans to unveil the car this October.

The renders show a sleek, modern interior divided by a central bar that runs the full length of the car. This makes the Type 01 a four-seat car with distinct seating areas for each of the passengers.

Another notable aspect of the interior is the lack of a giant, central screen – commonly seen in modern electric cars.

A small screen is mounted on the central division, while other "digital interfaces are intelligently applied for control on demand".

"Our holistic design philosophy translates the vehicle's exterior presence into a distinctive interior architecture," said Jaguar's chief interior designer Thomas Holden.

"In contrast to the horizontal interior design norm, we emphasise its dramatic longitudinal nature through the central spine – an architectural statement that creates four individual spaces," he continued.

"With authentic materials, technology on demand and reductive flowing surfaces, Type 01 presents unmistakable drama and theatre that will define the modern luxury automotive interior of the future."

A prototype of the Type 01 will be on display at this week's Monterey Car Week.

The car will be the first released by Jaguar as part of its "complete reset" as it moves to electric-only cars. The reset began with a controversial rebrand at the end of 2024.

Read:

Jaguar's controversial Type 00 concept car spotted driving on the streets of Paris

"Jaguar Type 01 is the first production car to follow our new creative philosophy," said Jaguar managing director Rawdon Glover.

"Unmistakable from every angle, the interior is no different. With Type 01, we wanted every journey to be an occasion, from how it drives to how it looks and how it makes you feel.

"With a confidence-inspiring GT driving position, clean and sophisticated technology and dramatic styling, Type 01 has an interior like no other."

The reset was led by Jaguar Land Rover chief creative officer Gerry McGovern, who departed the company at the end of 2025, a year after the unveiling of the radical Type 00 concept car.

item.content:encoded:
British eyewear brand Cubitts has unveiled its first shop in Manchester, designed by locally based studio Youth to reflect the city's industrial and musical history without resorting to the obvious.

Youth co-founders Oliver Collinge and Liam McGroarty planned the interior to reflect the present and future of the British city, with subtle references to the past rather than cliches.

It includes a shelving display combining tubular steel uprights with dapple-textured glass shelves, a faceted oak counter housing a till and record player, and a pair of figurative sandstone sculptures by artist Richard Perry.

The designers aimed to create a space "that feels both familiar and distinctly contemporary".

"Inspired by the city itself, the space draws on Manchester's culture and historic character, reinterpreted through a contemporary lens," they said.

The approach reflects the brief set by Cubitts founder Tom Broughton "to make the space feel distinctly Cubitts without resorting to the usual Manchester shorthand".

"It was important that Cubitts Manchester was designed in Manchester, and not just deposited here," Broughton said.

"Manchester does not need another London brand telling it how interesting it is. We're simply pleased to finally be here, and hope to make ourselves useful."

The store is located in Smithfield Buildings in the Northern Quarter, a collection of buildings that once housed the Affleck & Brown department store, dubbed the 'Harrods of the North'.

After more than a decade looking at locations, Broughton and his team chose this one for its history as a supplier of cloth and made-to-measure garments.

Read:

EBBA Architects transforms former jellied-eel restaurant into eyewear store

This aligns with Cubitts' own approach, with facilities for eye examinations, spectacle repairs and customisation made visible in the store.

"Smithfield Buildings felt immediately right: a spectacle shop inside a former draper's department store, in a neighbourhood shaped by making, music and independent trade," said Broughton.

Waxed cotton curtains softly divide different areas in tribute to Affleck & Brown's legacy, while other additions include a vintage revolving bookcase.

Produced by Manchester cabinetmakers Goodall, Lamb and Heighway, this century-old piece was made with salvaged timber from the Royal Navy ship HMS Foudroyant.

Artworks also hint at industrial production; a seamstress is depicted in a painting by artist Francis Hoyland, while a cubist gouache by artist Marcel Gille depicts a forge worker.

Completing the design are dimpled mirrors that offer slightly cloudy reflections and a collection of records spanning soul, jazz, punk and electronica.

Cubitts Manchester is the brand's 21st location, following others that include the peep-show-inspired Cubitts Soho and the art-deco-style Cubitts Leeds.

The company also just unveiled a new headquarters in London's King's Cross, in a historic building that began as a working stable for the Crosse & Blackwell Vinegar Works, before being converted into an office for a publishing house.

The photography is courtesy of Cubitts.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Kii has designed an ice cream shop on Miyakojima Island, Japan, featuring a pink ceiling, a limestone counter and perforated concrete tiles.

Called SR Ice Cream Miyakojima, the cafe and ice cream shop is located on an island in the southern part of Japan's Okinawa prefecture in the Pacific Ocean.

Its ocean-side setting influenced the interior, which features local materials chosen for their weather resistance.

"On Miyakojima Island, its local residents, new arrivals and tourists coexist and the goal was to create a welcoming environment where people of all backgrounds can simply drop by to enjoy a shared atmosphere over an ice cream or coffee," Kii co-founder Satoshi Arai told Dezeen.

"To withstand Miyakojima's subtropical oceanic climate, materials were also carefully selected to ensure finishes which are both functional and enduring," Arai continued.

The centrepiece of SR Ice Cream Miyakojima is a large, rounded counter made from limestone and with a lime plaster tabletop, around which customers can stand or sit.

Kii worked with an Okinawan plaster specialist to design the counter.

"Work to the counter involves applying rounded lumps of limestone clay – Ryukyu limestone, a local material in Miyakojima – to the counter surface one piece at a time," Kii co-founder Kei Nakatomi told Dezeen.

"The process of applying this material repeatedly creates a layered finish, and allows its unique texture to truly stand out," Nakatomi continued.

"The tabletop was also crafted using the same limestone clay and polished to reveal the material's unique texture."

Kii also inserted a playful arched door in the counter to create easy access for filter maintenance.

Above the central counter, Kii added a curved ceiling designed to draw visitors' attention and make the counter an attraction in itself.

Read:

Funamachi Base cafe and sweet shop designed as "extension of the park"

The studio chose a pale pink hue for the ceiling, in response to the natural light of the cafe's surroundings.

"Considering the dramatic shifts in natural light throughout the day on Miyakojima, we tested several options on-site to determine the ideal colour – ultimately selecting this specific shade of pink – to ensure it harmonised with the environment at any time of day or night," Arai said.

The salt air and harsh sunlight on the island influenced Arai and Nakatomi's choice of materials, and the two designers also aimed to showcase artisanal craftsmanship from different regions of Japan.

Apart from the limestone counter, one of the most noticeable materials in the SR ice cream shop is a specific type of concrete brick, which is perforated with holes for typhoon-struck areas.

"In the Okinawa area, where typhoons frequently hit, concrete blocks with holes are in use for architecture," Nakatomi said.

"When considering how to incorporate this unique characteristic of the region as an element that would blend seamlessly into the interior, custom tiles by Tajimi Tiles were selected."

The studio also added cushions woven from Cogon grass, which is native to the island, and colourful glazed stools by NOTA shop in Shigaraki – an old pottery area.

These pastel stools were specially chosen for the ice cream store as they had to be easy to maintain and have a non-directional design to fit under low tables.

"We picked the stool regularly produced by NOTA shop, with an original glazed colour on it," Arai said. "We designed these with the mindset of embracing the unpredictable results over its final appearance, and enjoyed the process of letting the results surprise us."

Kii did have some input into the glazing, as the studio wanted the stools to resemble ice cream that had started to melt.

"We did, however, go through a number of prototypes to fine-tune the glaze, aiming for a colour and texture that's reminiscent of melting ice cream," Arai added.

Overall, the studio said the ice cream shop, which sits on the ground floor of an ocean-side commercial development, has become the type of place that it envisioned when coming up with the design.

"We had heard that many guests would linger or stick around, whilst being engaged with guests inside or outside – just like a community, and as the type of space we had imagined while we had designed it," Nakatomi said.

Other Japanese cafes recently covered on Dezeen include a cafe and brewery on Teshima Island and a Blue Bottle Coffee cafe informed by Osaka Castle.

The photography is by Masanori Kaneshita.

item.content:encoded:
Texas architecture studio Clayton Korte has completed a Corten steel-clad structure for storing vineyard equipment at a winery on the Central Coast of California.

The 4,315-square-foot (400-square-metre) barn serves a 150-acre vineyard in Cayucos, a town in California's Santa Lucia Range. The barn sits between a working Syrah vineyard to the west and an oak forest to the east.

A simple plan with a gabled roof, the structure serves as a mediator between cultivated and natural landscapes.

"The structure opens westward with broad bays that frame the vineyard and tie the building directly to the daily rhythm of harvest and cultivation, while the forested hillside grounds it to the east," Clayton Korte principal Brian Korte told Dezeen.

The plan is organised around functionality for farm operations. Sliding doors at each end allow for easy mobility, while five bay doors open for manoeuvring equipment and work as cover for a generous porch area for outdoor work.

To accommodate the rural, off-grid site for wildfire, the studio clad the wood-framed structure entirely in weathering steel – corrugated on the roof and long sides and smooth on the short sides – that will resist fires, age gracefully and reduce long-term maintenance.

"Materials for a barn need to be practical, robust and not too precious, while also bringing their own authenticity and simple elegance to a structure," Korte said.

"They are honest and perform the dual task of serving both structural requirements and architectural finishes in many cases."

"The foggy marine layer that rolls through this landscape becomes part of the architecture, deepening the steel's natural patina over time so the building settles into, rather than stands apart from, the vineyards and hillsides around it."

Mesh screens extend out of the gabled ends, finishing out the building's profile with a translucent film and complementing the sliding doors that were salvaged from the local Saxum Winery.

Inside, the wooden frame and raw plywood panelling were left exposed to allow for the building's use to be adapted over time, and the fluted-glazed overhead doors provide an unexpected detail to the agricultural structure, washing the interior in daylight while keeping the form simple and utilitarian.

Read:

Clayton Korte creates "familiar yet exclusive" winery buildings in California

"In a project like this, it's the small moves that matter most – subtle shifts in orientation, material transitions and moments of openness that create a deeper dialogue with the land," said Clayton Korte senior architect Josh Nieves.

"Nothing is loud, but everything is deliberate."

Operating entirely off-grid, the barn's photovoltaic panels charge an on-site battery bank that manages lighting and power for operations, eliminating any reliance on external utilities.

"Sustainability isn't just about systems – it's about restraint and respect," Korte said.

"By building off the grid, using reclaimed elements and allowing materials to weather naturally, we let the structure quietly support the land rather than compete with it."

Clayton Korte, which has offices in Austin and San Antonio and was formerly known as Clayton & Little, has worked on wineries across California and Texas.

In the last few years, the 25-person studio has completed a pair of polycarbonate and steel buildings for Fulldraw Vineyard and a breezy, weathering steel barn for the Saxum Vineyard, both in Paso Robles, California, as well as a wine cave embedded in limestone outside of Austin.

The photography is by Casey Dunn and Ray Castro.
